To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

attendance and quality of parental participation in parent management treatment are related to changes in parental perceptions and behaviors and that these changes in turn predict changes in children's conduct problems.
quality of participation in a parent management training program is more important than attendance for treatment outcome.
quality of parent participation is related to treatment outcome, but attendance is not, and quality of participation can be predicted from family characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How do family characteristics and participation in parent training predict changes in parenting?
the role that family and child characteristics play in the success of a parent management training program.
the development of interventions to prevent the onset of antisocial behavior in children and adolescents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quality of participation in a treatment program is a stronger predictor of the outcome of that treatment than is the mere fact of attendance at the program.
attendance is a necessary but not sufficient predictor of treatment response in parent management training.
attendance is important, but quality of participation is even more important.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is necessary to understand how to help families participate in the process of change.
it is not only important to get parents to come to treatment, but it is also important to get them to actively engage in the treatment.
we found that parent management training was effective, that it was most effective for parents who were most engaged, and that it was most engaged for parents who were least disadvantaged.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not sufficient to get parents to simply attend sessions; it also matters how they participate in the therapeutic process.
it is not sufficient for families to simply show up to treatment sessions.
we should not assume that attendance in treatment predicts treatment outcome.
